Title: Recursive source walk and diff
Detail: Walks the source tree recursively and records one index row per file (SR-001). A pure comparison of those rows against the backup's index returns two sets that the run then acts on: the files that are new or changed, and the files removed from the source.

Title: XXH128 file hashing
Detail: Hashes a file's full content with XXH128, streaming it rather than loading it whole, and renders the digest as 32 uppercase hex characters in big-endian byte order (SR-002). The hashing library is guaranteed loaded before the first hash is taken.

Title: Content-addressed dedup keying
Detail: Groups the source rows by (xxH2Hash, Length) and stores the physical data once per key (SR-003). The stored object's name is derived from its content under the SR-069 grammar; every row of a group after the first is marked Duplicate.

Title: Already-compressed list and 7-Zip storage
Detail: One list, defined in exactly one place, names the file extensions known to be already compressed (archives, disk images, video, audio, image and packed-container formats). It is the accepted-known-formats fast path, not an attempt at completeness: office and text formats are not on it because they are not known to be already compressed, and a filesystem container such as .iso is excluded because listing it would wrongly call its contents compressed. Its answer is an input to the storage-form decision (LLR-086), taken as if compression were enabled so it carries only the list's opinion; it is the whole decision only with the probe off or below the probe's size floor. The engine holds no copy of the list; it asks the shared library. The user-facing documentation's table of already-compressed extensions is kept equal to the live list. Writing a compressed object first removes any existing object at the destination name, because the archiver adds to an existing archive rather than replacing it: the write path trusts only the index, so an unreferenced object at that content-derived name (left by a run killed before its index was written, by a row evicted while its object awaits prune, or by an interrupted archiver) would otherwise be merged into the new object. The archive is written at the 7-Zip compression level resolved once from FILEBACKUP_7Z_LEVEL (LLR-037), 9 unless the operator sets otherwise. The shared library publishes the resolved level and any rejected raw value, so the entry point can refuse an invalid value without reaching into the library's internal state, and the library still depends on nothing in the engine.

Title: Dated snapshot completion
Detail: Builds the snapshot in the staging area and, when the run changed the index's state, publishes it under the name Snapshot_<prior-backup-date> only after its own index is written (SR-005). Whether the state changed is decided from the source-versus-backup diff being non-empty, not from the count of physical copies, which misses additions served by deduplication and removals of shared content. A run whose index is identical produces no snapshot, and the latest (live) state is never a snapshot. Two snapshots dated to the same second are kept apart by a disambiguating suffix. The snapshot's date is injectable so tests can date it deterministically.

Title: Refcount-aware eviction
Detail: Evicts a removed file's data to staging only when no surviving manifest row references its (hash,size) (SR-006); shared data is retained (B9).

Title: Restore-kit deposition
Detail: Deposits the restore kit into the live backup and into each dated snapshot (SR-007): the PowerShell restorer, the shell restorer, the shared library, the hashing library, the paths sidecar, and the two launchers (RECONSTRUCT.cmd and reconstruct.command, copied beside the shell restorer). The shared library imports nothing from the engine, a load-bearing split that keeps the kit self-contained. The Windows launcher is a pure passthrough with no pause. The retired launcher name RECONSTRUCT.bat is never written but is still recognised as infrastructure, so an older store's leftover copy is not reported as an orphan (SR-022).

Title: Standalone reconstruction
Detail: Rebuilds the tree from the index using only the bundled shared library (SR-008). A row whose stored object is an archive is expanded; a row with a blank DataPath is recovered by scanning the pool for a content-hash match.

Title: Restore target guard
Detail: Rejects a restore target located inside the backup folder before writing any file, and refuses any manifest row whose canonicalized destination falls outside the target root — the row is warned, counted unrestored, and fails the run per SR-029 (SR-009).

Title: Point-in-time restore authority
Detail: When launched from a Snapshot_<date> folder, the restorer uses that snapshot's own index as the sole authority, with no overlay from a newer index, and resolves bytes by (xxH2Hash, Length) over the data pool: the backup root plus every snapshot folder (SR-010). The pool scan skips infrastructure names only at a folder's root (SR-022); a nested file with an infrastructure name is data and a legitimate recovery source (B6). Matching is by (hash, length), so the skip is an optimisation, not a correctness gate.

Title: Rehash scheduling decision
Detail: Maps the rehash frequency (A/E/D/W/M/Y/N), the last rehash time and an injectable current time to a single decision: recalculate or not (SR-011). The last rehash time is persisted per set in the backup's run-state record.

Title: Per-set isolation and exit code
Detail: The entry point processes each configured set in turn and folds each set's outcome into one overall result (SR-014). A set's failure is logged without aborting the remaining sets, and any failed set makes the process exit 1.

Title: Conditional non-fatal mail
Detail: Sends the run's mail only when the SMTP fields are present and -NoMail is not given (SR-015). A mail-send failure is caught and logged as WARN and never changes the exit status (B15).

Title: Non-interactive automation path
Detail: -NonInteractive on the backup entry point reaches tool resolution and hashing-library loading, so an unattended run never blocks on a prompt (SR-016): a missing optional tool degrades to absent, and a missing hashing library is either auto-installed (when asked) or fails with guidance. The PowerShell restorer accepts -NonInteractive too. When no restore target is given and the run is non-interactive, or its input is redirected, the restorer prints its usage, matching the shell restorer's usage parameter for parameter, and exits 2 (usage/precondition), as the shell restorer already does for its required target argument; the interactive prompt is kept for hand use. The Windows launcher passes all its arguments through, so it needs no change for this. The decision whether to prompt, and how, is a pure function returning None, Text or Gui; None also covers a session with neither an interactive console nor a desktop, which would otherwise block forever on a text prompt.

Title: Stale staging: classify, reclaim or refuse
Detail: A run that finds a staging area already present under the change root never overwrites it. Creating the staging area is the fast path and is unchanged for a healthy run; classification is reached only when the create fails and the staging area exists as a directory, and any other create failure is logged verbatim and re-raised. Classification takes a forced, literal, fail-closed listing of the staging area and the owner record (LLR-080), and on the Empty and OwnerStale verdicts the caller takes the confirmation sample itself, so the classifier stays pure. The confirmation wait is at least 90 s, lengthened to the record's own declared heartbeat cadence plus 30 s, and capped at 600 s. Only a confirmed-stale area is reclaimed, by this exact protocol: move it aside to Temp.stale-<utc>-<8 hex>; re-examine the moved folder against the sampled identity, and if it is live move it straight back and refuse; create a fresh staging area and immediately write this run's owner record, closing the reclaimer's own create-to-marker window; then re-list the aside folder, delete only the exact marker by name, and delete the folder non-recursively. Nothing in this path deletes recursively; if either delete fails the folder is kept and the documented recovery is printed, and a failed move refuses without retrying in a loop. Every other verdict refuses with its own token: [SR-075/owner-live], [SR-075/content-refused], [SR-075/prune-held]; Indeterminate, or a staging area that is a reparse point, refuses with the content token. The refusal message states its reason without hedging. On success the run writes its owner record as soon as the staging area exists and keeps a rooted heartbeat handle with it. All work after acquisition runs inside a guard that always stops and drains the heartbeat, so an exception after the staging area gains content cannot leave a live heartbeat advertising an abandoned lock as owned; that guard only stops the heartbeat and deletes nothing. A run cleans up its own staging area only after proving the area is still its own: the marker is present and carries this run's id, and nothing is inside beyond the marker and this run's own early staging artifacts (the copied prior index, its witness and the directory sidecar, none of them a unique copy, which is what lets a late capacity refusal release its own lock instead of stranding the staging area). It then stops and drains the heartbeat, deletes those exact leaves by name with the marker last, and removes the folder non-recursively; on any doubt it keeps the folder and logs [SR-075/lock-lost]. Either way the original error is re-raised. This prevents a resurrected owner's ordinary failure from recursively deleting its successor's staging area. The run re-reads the marker and compares the run id at five boundaries: before writing the staging copy of the index, before evicting removed files, before preserving superseded data, before publishing the backup root's index and witness, and before publishing the snapshot. An unreadable marker is retried three times about 300 ms apart; a mismatch is never retried and aborts the run, cleaning up nothing. Immediately before the snapshot is published the run stops and drains the heartbeat and removes its marker, because publishing either deletes the staging area or turns it wholesale into a snapshot, and a surviving marker would be published into every snapshot and then refused by prune's unreferenced-data rail (SR-046). The whole create, classification, confirmation sample and any reclaim run under the staging OS lock (LLR-090), taken before the staging area is touched; a lock that cannot be taken refuses the set first. The held lock is passed to classification and reclaim only to be logged: every verdict and refusal above is unchanged by it, because an older FileBackup takes no OS lock. The lock is released when staging setup fails, or at the very end after the heartbeat is stopped, never before the snapshot is published.

Title: Missing-config guard
Detail: Checks that the configuration path names an existing file, not a directory, and refuses before any work with a message naming the missing path ("Config file '<path>' not found.") (SR-018).

Title: External-tool resolution
Detail: Locates the configured external tools. A missing 7-Zip fails before any set that needs compression is processed; a missing ffprobe leaves the media-rate metric blank (SR-020).

Title: Literal/bracket-safe paths
Detail: Every file operation treats a path literally: wildcard metacharacters such as brackets are never interpreted, and path splitting into parent and leaf is done without an operation that fails on PowerShell 7, so Unicode and bracketed names stay intact (SR-021). A generated object name cannot contain a wildcard metacharacter at all (SR-069), so only source-derived paths depend on this.

Title: Root-only infrastructure test
Detail: Classifies kit and index names as infrastructure only at the backup root (SR-022); a nested user file with the same name is data (B6). The allowlist covers every artifact the restore kit deposits, including the paths sidecar.

Title: Restore capacity check
Detail: Before restoring anything, the restorer compares the bytes the restore needs against the target volume's free space and refuses with the precondition code when they do not fit (SR-023, B10/B11). The sum counts the recorded lengths of rows stored uncompressed and leaves out compressed rows, logging that the true need is higher when any exist. The target volume is measured in a way that works for a drive-qualified Windows path, a UNC path and a rooted POSIX path alike, so the check is never silently inert on Linux or in a container. An unmeasurable volume skips the check rather than refusing.

Title: Deterministic manifest output
Detail: Stable row ordering + typed serialization make an unchanged re-run produce byte-identical manifest rows (SR-024).

Title: Manifest schema round-trip
Detail: One reader and one writer are the only I/O for the 9-column index schema. They preserve typed Length and LastWriteTime, tolerate null or empty cells, and return an empty set for a missing index (SR-025). The writer publishes the index atomically: a reader sees either the previous complete index or the new complete one, never a partial write (SR-082, LLR-087).

Title: Cross-change duplicate collapse
Detail: After a run, collapses identical data shared across change folders to a single stored copy that each folder can still resolve (SR-026). The blanking pass re-reads and rewrites only a change folder whose DataPaths name a vanished file; a folder whose DataPaths all still exist is neither re-read nor rewritten. Each distinct DataPath of a change folder is probed exactly once, in one complete pass that collects the vanished ones into an ordinal set; rows are then blanked by membership in that set, with no second probe. The folder's index is read only when something vanished, and only when the content index does not already hold its rows.

Title: Dated-snapshot storage and clean cutover
Detail: Persists each set's last backup-completion time in the run-state record and uses it to date the next snapshot. A snapshot keeps the full pre-run index plus only the superseded bytes, deduplicated across snapshots (LLR-026). Snapshot folders are recognised by the single ^Snapshot_ pattern shared by the engine and both restorers (SR-028). The completion time is injectable so tests can build deterministic timelines. Run state (last rehash and last backup) is persisted after the snapshot is published and before the cross-change deduplication, so a kill during deduplication cannot leave it stale.

Title: Config builder and quick-start
Detail: A configuration builder plus the README quick-start let a new user produce a valid configuration document and run a first backup (SR-027); the hashing library installs itself on first use.

Title: Reconstruct unrestored-row accounting
Detail: The restore loop records every row it skips (blank-DataPath hash-recovery failure, missing DataPath, extraction failure) instead of silently continuing. After the loop, a non-empty list logs an INCOMPLETE summary and fails the run, so a scripted caller sees a non-zero exit (SR-029). A clean run exits 0.

Title: Shell XXH128 wrapper
Detail: The shell restorer hashes a file through the system's XXH128 tool (xxhsum or xxh128sum, whichever is present) and normalises the output to the same 32-character uppercase big-endian hex the PowerShell side emits (SR-030). The wrapper lives inside the single self-contained shell restorer, which sources no runtime libraries, and the script can be loaded without running its main body so the function can be exercised on its own.

Title: Shell standalone restorer
Detail: The shell restorer restores from the backup root or from a Snapshot_<date> folder with the SR-031 semantics, mirroring the PowerShell restorer: it selects its authority from its own folder's name (the ^Snapshot_ pattern); parses the index as RFC-4180 CSV; maps RelativePath backslashes to '/'; recovers blank or missing-DataPath rows by hash over the data pool (the backup root plus every snapshot); expands rows whose stored object is an archive; refuses a target inside the backup; checks capacity before writing; and accounts for unrestored rows, exiting non-zero with the count (as SR-029 requires). It is a single self-contained file, and its tool preflight fails loudly with remediation (the SN-015 pattern).

Title: Manifest portability layer
Detail: The shell restorer parses the index as RFC-4180 CSV, handling quoted fields with commas and embedded quotes, and tolerates a UTF-8 BOM; it maps RelativePath backslashes to '/'; and it treats LastWriteTimeStr as opaque ISO-8601 round-trip text that is never reparsed or reformatted. Both functions live inside the self-contained shell restorer (SR-032).

Title: Shell backup engine
Detail: A shell backup engine produces backups that conform to the store contract and interoperate with the PowerShell engine (SR-033): the 9-column index schema, deduplication by content, object names under the shared grammar (SR-069), the composed storage-form decision (LLR-086), dated snapshots and reference-counted eviction.

Title: Run-state integrity gate
Detail: Before any mutation, a backup run reads the prior backup date and refuses when it is absent while the existing index still has rows; an unparseable run-state record is a failure, never an empty first-run state. A non-initial run therefore can never take the first-backup publishing branch, which would discard staged history (SR-035).

Title: Empty-source refusal
Detail: When the source scan returns no files for a source whose backup index still has rows, the run removes its own staging area and refuses the set unless the set's AllowEmptySource is true; the error names the surviving row count and the override key (SR-036).

Title: Portable tool resolution
Detail: The default 7-Zip location comes from FILEBACKUP_7ZIP_PATH; failing that, on Windows the standard install location, and failing that the first 7-Zip command found on the PATH. Resolving it never throws on a non-Windows host. A set's Tools.SevenZipPath takes precedence over the default, and the missing-7-Zip remediation names both settings (SR-037). The same import-time resolution reads FILEBACKUP_7Z_LEVEL into the 7-Zip compression level, accepting only the ten single-digit strings '0' to '9' by exact membership: no trimming, so a padded or whitespace-only value is invalid, while an absent or empty variable simply means the default, 9. This resolution never throws, because the restorers import the same shared library and a bad environment variable must not break a restore; instead it records the raw rejected value and leaves the level at 9. The backup entry point checks that record immediately after the configuration loads and before the run creates any artifact (the global log directory included), and refuses with the configuration-failure status (2 under -ExitCode, SR-042/SR-043) when the value is invalid AND -Action is Backup AND some set has CompressEnabled true. Verify, View, Prune, Snapshots, a run where every set has compression off, and both restorers are therefore unaffected by the variable.

Title: Witness sidecar writer
Detail: The index writer publishes the index atomically (SR-082, LLR-087) and then writes its witness: the XXH128 digest of the written index, emitted as Version/Rows/Bytes/XxH128/Written key=value lines, UTF-8 without BOM, LF line endings, written to a temporary sidecar in the same folder and published by an atomic rename over any prior witness. The witness writer lives in the shared library because the PowerShell restorer may use only that library (AGENTS.md section 3). The witness file name joins the root-level infrastructure allowlist beside the paths sidecar, together with the two temporary names MANIFEST.csv.meta.tmp and MANIFEST.csv.tmp: a crash between writing and publishing leaves a temporary file behind, and a leftover must neither be backed up as user data nor warned about as an orphan. The row count comes from the writer, which already holds the records it wrote, rather than from re-reading the index; a standalone re-stamp of the witness counts the file instead. A snapshot inherits its own witness because its staged index is rewritten through the same writer before the snapshot is published; the witness is deliberately not in the kit-artifact copy list, which would overwrite the snapshot's witness with the backup root's (SR-038).

Title: Restore-side witness verification
Detail: A shared-library verifier reads the witness, compares Bytes, Rows and XxH128 against the index on disk, and returns a verdict (Verified, Absent, Mismatch or Malformed) with the failing field and an optional non-fatal warning. Fields are checked Bytes, then Rows, then XxH128, but a Rows-only disagreement defers to the digest: when bytes and digest match, the index IS the witnessed one, so it verifies with a warning (counting-semantics divergence) rather than aborting; with no digest present, a row-count disagreement still aborts. Both restorers verify after confirming the index exists and before creating the target folder, the restore log or running the capacity pre-check, so an exit-2 or exit-3 refusal writes nothing into the target (log lines are buffered and flushed once the log exists). The PowerShell restorer also checks the index's CSV header shape, as the shell restorer already does, and the shell restorer verifies at the same point, immediately after its header check. An absent witness warns and continues unless -RequireWitness / --require-witness is given (SR-039).

Title: Restore exit-code taxonomy
Detail: The pool locator in both restorers returns one cause per lookup: Found, ContentMissing, DependencyMissing or StorageUnreadable, with a detail. Search folders are probed for existence and readability. An archive candidate met without a usable 7-Zip yields DependencyMissing; a candidate that cannot be read at all is the host condition StorageUnreadable and records exactly that one cause, never DependencyMissing as well; a candidate that fails to expand is data damage, folded into the ContentMissing detail (' ; N candidate(s) could not be expanded: <first>'). The locator never returns CandidateError. Whether an expand failure counts as damage is gated by a self-test that 7-Zip is actually usable. The restore loop records each unrestored row with its cause and detail; its own CandidateError (the row's own file failed to expand or copy) and WriteMismatch stay host-class. The summary classifies unrestored rows into the content class (exit 1) and the host class (exit 4). Both restorers report an unlistable snapshot tree as StorageUnreadable (exit 4) rather than silently shrinking the recovery pool. Under -ExitCode (which the Windows launcher passes) a classified outcome becomes the process exit code; otherwise it raises an error carrying the same message wording, so in-process callers keep working. Any terminating error the restorer did not classify is routed to the precondition class (exit 2 under -ExitCode, re-raised otherwise), so an unexpected failure can never be reported as data loss (1). Failures creating the target folder or the restore log route through the same class, matching the shell restorer's refusal (2) for a file occupying the target path. The shell restorer reports usage and precondition failures as 2, the witness refusal as 3, and the 1-versus-4 split at the end of its run; its usage text and header comment carry the exit-code table (SR-040).

Title: Move-loop failure aggregation
Detail: Evicting removed files and preserving superseded data each catch a failure per file (including creating the destination directory), log 'Failed to <evict|preserve> ...: <message>' at ERROR, record the entry, mark the run unsuccessful and continue; each reports a summary count, so a partially staged snapshot is explicit. The run then still proceeds to publish the snapshot, so the staging area is never orphaned (SR-017) (SR-041).

Title: Validating configuration loader
Detail: The configuration loader belongs to the backup-only engine, not the shared library, because configuration loading has no restore-side meaning and the library must stay restore-safe. It accepts the JSON and the CLIXML configuration document, chosen by file extension. JSON: ConfigVersion must be an integer within [1, the current schema version], range-checked before any integer conversion, so an out-of-range version is refused as unsupported rather than by luck of fractional representation. The key set is closed at the top level, under Tools, under Secrets and in each set, and Secrets.Credential is refused explicitly. Type checks read the parsed JSON value's actual type, so a quoted "false" is refused rather than coerced to true; an 'integer' accepts any integral-valued JSON number, culture-safely and including one beyond the 64-bit range. CLIXML: the shape check only, keeping its established message wording. Both formats run the same shape and value checks. Defaults are materialised for every set: SourceStatePath defaults to SourcePath, AllowEmptySource to false, CompressProbe to always, and HashRecalcFreq is upper-cased. Every validated optional key reaches the engine; a validated key must never be silently dropped during defaulting. CompressProbe's vocabulary is exact lowercase (off, excluded-extensions, always), so a mixed-case 'Always' is refused, and the value check runs for both formats, which makes it the only place an invalid CLIXML value is caught. Errors are terminating, single, first in document order, and name the JSON path; a set is named by its real array index. A published draft-07 JSON schema with additionalProperties:false mirrors the validator, including the CompressProbe enum, the BackupSets shape and the ConfigVersion constant. It is documentation, not read at runtime, and is not shipped in the container image. ConfigVersion stays 2 for an optional, defaulted key: such an addition is additive (SR-063). The key is documented in the entry point's help and example configuration, the README field table and IF-001 (SR-042).

Title: Entry-point status codes
Detail: The backup entry point accepts -ExitCode. A configuration failure, including a missing or unreadable configuration file, writes its message to stderr and, with -ExitCode, exits 2; without it the error is re-raised so in-process callers still see it. A failed set exits 1 in both modes. The container entry point passes -ExitCode ahead of the caller's arguments. The codes match the restorers' table (0 complete, 1 incomplete, 2 usage/precondition), so one vocabulary covers both halves of IF-001 (SR-043). The run's log is not created until the configuration has loaded successfully, because creating the log truncates it, and creating it earlier destroyed the previous run's log on a configuration typo. Configuration-time messages, such as the multi-set warning, are buffered and flushed once the log exists. A configuration failure appends to the global log only when that file already exists, and creates nothing.

Title: Prune plan and re-homed copy
Detail: The prune plan builds the pool's content index (LLR-047) and derives the demand set: every row outside the target whose DataPath is blank, or whose non-blank DataPath names a file that is absent (verification can blank root DataPaths in a damaged store). It emits one plan item per endangered key, naming its source location and row, its destination folder, name and row, its stored form and its bytes. The destination is elected as cross-change deduplication elects it: the backup root when it demands the key, otherwise the newest demanding snapshot by folder order. The destination name IS the source row's DataPath: a stored object's name derives from its content and stored form, so a re-homed object's name is always identical to its source's. A name that would classify as root-level infrastructure at the destination, or that would overwrite a DIFFERENT file already there, is recorded as a code-2 problem instead of an item; an identical file already there is treated as an interrupted prune's completed copy, and the prune resumes. A re-homed copy is written to '<destination>.fbprune.tmp', path taken literally, and verified for stored-form identity (length and XXH128 equal to the source) and, unless content verification is skipped, for content identity against the row's xxH2Hash and Length, expanding an archive to a temporary file first, the same check the restorers' pool locator makes. It is then published by rename. Publishing the plan mutates only DataPath, Compressed and StoredAsHashSize on the destination row and persists through the one index writer, so the witness (SR-038) is re-stamped by its one writer and is never copied between folders.

Title: Prune rails, pool proof and commit point
Detail: The prune precondition check returns the full set of refusals, each with a code, kind and message, rather than stopping at the first; the prune applies the precedence 2 > 3 > 4 > 1 over the whole set, and a -WhatIf run can report every refusal at once. It checks: - the target is an existing ^Snapshot_ folder that is a direct child of the resolved change root and contains no wildcard (2); - the SR-035 run-state gate: a malformed run-state record, or a populated backup index with no last-backup time (2); - no staging area in the change root (2, mutual exclusion with a backup, SR-017); - the plan's own code-2 problems (unknown target, infrastructure name, destination collision); - no unreferenced data files in the target, measured against the target's own index, unless -DiscardUnreferencedData (2); - the WHOLE pool resolves, so an already-broken pool or a pre-existing form disagreement refuses rather than being pruned into (2); - free space on each destination volume for the planned bytes, grouped by volume identity so a UNC or rooted POSIX store is checked too; an unmeasurable volume is skipped rather than refused (2); - 7-Zip present when the plan carries a compressed row and content verification is on (2); - the witness of EVERY pool index: Mismatch or Malformed (3), Absent (3) unless -AllowUnverifiedIndex. The pool-resolution check rebuilds the index over the pool minus an excluded folder and reports every row that would not resolve, plus every form disagreement: Compressed='Yes' with a located file that is not '.7z', or Compressed='No' with a located '.7z' file whose row's RelativePath is not itself '.7z' (which would be a legitimately stored already-compressed source file). Deletion renames the folder to 'Pruning_<name>', which is the commit point because that name matches neither the engine's snapshot pattern nor either restorer's ^Snapshot_ pattern, and then deletes it recursively. Residue is handled in two parts. Committed residue, 'Pruning_<that same name>' only, is removed before the named snapshot is planned: it is past the commit point, invisible to every consumer, and holds the name the plan needs; a host failure there is a code-4 record, not an unclassified error, and the step is skipped under -WhatIf. The entry sweep runs inside the transaction, after the rails pass and the staging lock is held, so a refusal mutates nothing and a sweep failure is code 4; it scans only pool folders (the backup root and Snapshot_*) and deletes a '*.fbprune.tmp' only when that folder's own index does not reference it, because a staged copy is unreferenced by construction while a referenced file is content. The prune takes the staging area by creating it without overwrite: creation is the atomic test, closing the window between the staging-busy rail and the lock; an existing folder becomes the staging-busy refusal (code 2), and cleanup never deletes a lock this invocation did not create. The PRUNE.inprogress marker is written inside the transaction.

Title: Shared content index and snapshot inventory
Detail: The content index maps each '<xxH2Hash>|<Length>' key to the locations holding those bytes, each recording its folder, DataPath, full path, whether it is the backup root, and its folder order: the backup root first, then the given snapshot folders in the order supplied (name order, oldest first). It skips blank DataPaths, blank hashes and rows whose file is not on disk: the index describes bytes that EXIST, so a blank row is demand and never supply. It also returns one record per indexed folder. By default each folder record carries only the folder's identity, order and the non-blank DataPath values of its index in index order, and no whole index is retained: each index is read once, fed to the map and dropped, so the content index's memory grows with the number of stored objects, not with the rows of every snapshot. A caller that needs whole rows asks for the indexes to be retained; the prune plan and the pool-resolution check do, so prune still holds whole indexes. The storage-form audit uses the lean default: it reads each folder's index itself, one folder at a time. Cross-change deduplication uses the lean default: duplicate election is unchanged, and it re-reads and rewrites only a change folder whose DataPaths name a vanished file (LLR-026); it derives its list of change indexes from the same pass. The snapshot inventory lists the change root's folders matching the one snapshot pattern every consumer uses, sorted by name, and parses each snapshot's point-in-time date from its folder name, tolerating the same-second disambiguating suffix. The reported physical, reclaimable and re-homed bytes of a snapshot come straight from the prune plan, so the reported reclaim is the achieved reclaim by construction.

Title: Retention at the entry point and the container boundary
Detail: The backup entry point's -Action vocabulary includes Prune and Snapshots beside the default Backup, with -Snapshot naming the snapshots to act on. Prune and Snapshots resolve the single configured set's paths and either prune the named snapshots (passing -WhatIf through, with the resolved 7-Zip) or list the snapshot inventory as JSON. Under -ExitCode the SR-040 code from the batch result becomes the process exit code; otherwise a non-zero outcome raises an error for in-process callers. The Backup path is unchanged, so every existing invocation behaves exactly as before. The container entry point reads FILEBACKUP_ACTION, or takes a leading positional word in {backup, prune, snapshots}; anything starting with '-' is left in the arguments and flows through unchanged. FILEBACKUP_SNAPSHOT becomes -Snapshot and a truthy FILEBACKUP_DRY_RUN becomes -WhatIf. The shell restorer carries no removal path.

Title: Storage-form audit and repair
Detail: A stored file is classified as Archive or Raw from its first six bytes (the 7z signature 37 7A BC AF 27 1C) plus its extension, with no hashing. The storage-form audit walks the pool through the content index (LLR-047), the backup root first and then Snapshot_* in name order, and emits one finding per disagreement, naming the folder, RelativePath, DataPath, class, observed and expected form, and whether it is repairable. The classes are NameLies, FlagOverRaw, FlagOverArchive, DanglingDataPath, BlankRowFormDisagreement and Unreferenced. The already-compressed-source exemption is keyed on the payload, not the file name: when the observed form is Archive but the row says Compressed=No, the file's own bytes are hashed against the row's (xxH2Hash, Length); a match is correct raw storage of archive-shaped content and yields no finding, and only a mismatch is a genuine FlagOverArchive, because an already-compressed source can be named anything. A .7z RelativePath is the cheap fast path. The non-Deep scan widens that fast path for one shape only: a Compressed=No archive-signature object is exempt without hashing when all three hold: the row's RelativePath extension is one the already-compressed list exempts (asked of the shared library; the engine holds no copy of the list), its DataPath extension equals the row's RelativePath extension, and its on-disk length equals the row's Length. Without this, a store where a large share of objects are listed-format archives stored raw would be re-hashed in full on every non-Deep pass. The exemption proves form, not payload: a same-length substitution under a listed name passes the non-Deep scan and is caught by -Deep, the payload audit, which always hashes. An archive-signature object under a name the list does not exempt keeps the confirming hash. Otherwise the non-Deep scan reads six bytes per row. -Deep additionally verifies payload identity, and requires 7-Zip: a raw object by length and XXH128 against the row; an archive by its own bytes first, since for an already-compressed source stored raw those bytes ARE the payload, and only otherwise by expanding it to a temporary file and hashing. Repair acts only on findings whose evidence is a file in the row's own folder. It rewrites Compressed and renames the data file so name and form agree, never re-packs, never touches the six logical columns, and persists each folder through the one index writer. Findings are grouped by (folder, DataPath), so the physical rename happens once and every row referencing the old path adopts the observed form, including a row exempted by the payload-keyed rule, whose bytes' identity is read before the rename moves them (it follows the file and keeps its own Compressed). Blank-row findings are reported only. Enumeration recognises infrastructure only at each folder's own root (B6/SN-018). The outcome maps to the SR-040 table, and nothing in the backup run calls the audit. The verify entry point resolves the set's roots read-only, so verification creates no directory, does not require the source path, and reports a missing backup root as code 2. After a change to the already-compressed list or to the compression settings the pool can legitimately hold both forms of one (hash, length): content archived before the change and re-added raw after it. Cross-change deduplication keeps one copy and blanks the other snapshot row, whose recorded Compressed can then disagree with the surviving object; the resulting BlankRowFormDisagreement on that blanked row is expected and benign (reported only, never repaired), and restore is unaffected because both restorers decide the form from the file they locate.

Title: Hash recovery reports the located file's form
Detail: A pool lookup's Found result in both restorers also reports the located file's form: Archive when the match was proven by expanding an archive candidate, Raw when proven by hashing the file itself. When a row is recovered by hash, the restore loop records that form and decides whether to expand from it; a row with a non-blank DataPath is decided per LLR-068. Every archive candidate that does not yield the payload is re-tested as raw bytes (length and hash) before it is dropped, whether the expand failed (an archive name over raw content) or succeeded with other content (a genuine archive source file stored raw, whose own bytes are the row's content). If that raw-bytes test cannot read the file, the read failure is recorded once as StorageUnreadable and the candidate loop continues, since 7-Zip could not have helped read an unreadable file; only a candidate whose raw bytes were read successfully and did not match still records DependencyMissing when 7-Zip is unavailable. The shell restorer mirrors this, including the no-7-Zip arm. No new tool, state or index column is involved.

Title: Reference-counted deletion at every pool-removal site
Detail: Both steps that remove bytes from the pool, evicting removed files and preserving superseded data, ask the same question before removing anything: does any row of the FINAL index still claim this DataPath? (B9). A test based on the source rows instead cannot see a frozen row (SR-055/SR-057) or a row whose replacement copy failed, and would move out bytes those rows still claim. These two steps are the only pool-removal sites in a backup run, so the invariant lives entirely at them.

Title: Cross-platform free-space preflight
Detail: Free space is measured in the shared library, so the restore kit stays self-contained. The measurement resolves the path's containing volume from its full path, falls back to the drive for a drive-qualified path, and answers 'unknown' only when neither works; it never throws. Volume identity comes from the mount table: the longest real mount point that prefixes the resolved path on a separator boundary, so two paths on one POSIX mount (for example /backup and /backup/sub) are recognised as one volume. The PowerShell restorer's capacity check uses this, so SR-023 works for a rooted POSIX path. The backup capacity check sums the run's additions per volume: new (hash, length) groups the backup does not already hold, at uncompressed Length (a blank-DataPath row holds no bytes, so its heal copy is budgeted), plus the staging bytes only when the change root is on a different volume from the backup root. Demands on one volume are summed against that volume's free space, because checking them separately passed two demands that each fitted and together did not. A shortfall fails the set with a classified precondition failure (entry-point status 1) before any mutation: it is checked after the diff and before superseded data is preserved, the last point at which nothing has been written, so a refusal leaves none of this run's content written and no staging area orphaned. This is not a claim that the tree is byte-identical: nothing already stored is ever re-formed (SR-061), so there is nothing to migrate and nothing to size. An unmeasurable volume is skipped, not refused. There is no new configuration key (SR-042's schema is closed).

Title: Blank rows re-enter the diff; dedup adoption requires a non-blank DataPath
Detail: A row whose metadata equals the source but whose DataPath is blank counts as new-or-changed in the diff (a pure comparison). Deduplication adopts an existing stored object only from a row with a non-blank DataPath, so a (hash, length) group whose existing rows are all blank is copied afresh and every logical name in it, the healed row included, points at the newly written object. Preserving superseded data is unaffected: a heal row has the same content as its blank predecessor, so the same-content guard skips staging it.

Title: Verify runs the pool audit; the blank-row form rail is kit-revision-gated
Detail: -Action Verify runs the pool-resolution check alongside the storage-form audit, in the same guarded step, so a path failure stays code 2 and findings drive code 1. Each pool-resolution problem names its folder, RelativePath and DataPath and is reported as a finding: PoolDataPathMissing when the bytes still survive elsewhere in the pool (checked on disk against the content index, excluding the missing path itself), and PoolUnresolvable only for a row that genuinely has no bytes left. For a blank-DataPath row, a folder whose kit revision is 2 or higher skips the located-copy form comparison entirely, because that kit decides the form from the file (SR-050); below 2 the refusal remains, and its message names the kit revision and the -Action Verify -RefreshKits remedy. The backup capacity check does not count a blank-DataPath row as held, so heal copies are budgeted. The non-blank-DataPath form check is unchanged.

Title: Portable-name guard in the source scan
Detail: A relative path is classified per component as portable or not, returning nothing or a reason. On Windows both slashes separate components, elsewhere only '/'; a reserved device-name stem (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9, in any case, with or without an extension) is non-portable. The platform is injectable, so the POSIX-only backslash rule can be exercised on Windows. The source scan skips a non-portable name before trying to open or hash it and records its RelativePath and reason. The run logs one ERROR per record and marks the set failed, and leaves the skipped names out of the removed-from-source set, so an existing row is frozen rather than evicted.

Title: Restore verify-after-write and one-shot pool recovery
Detail: After a row's object is successfully expanded or copied, the restored file is hashed and its (Length, xxH2Hash) compared against the row. On a mismatch the file is deleted and the pool recovery by (hash, length) is attempted exactly once, as if the row had a blank DataPath, and the result is verified again. There is one verify implementation and one restore-this-row implementation in each restorer, called at most twice per row. No exclusion state is needed: the pool locator hashes every candidate itself, so a wrong-bytes file cannot be returned as a match. A row that still fails verification after the one recovery attempt is recorded as the content-class cause ContentMismatch, not as a host cause (SR-040/SR-056). When the locator proved its source and the written file still mismatches, the cause is the host-class WriteMismatch and there is no second search; a read-back failure is host-class and the file is kept.

Title: Hidden and dot entries captured at every enumeration
Detail: Every enumeration of the source, the pool and the change root includes hidden and system entries and descends into hidden directories: the source walk (including the cached-hash path), cross-change deduplication's scan of change folders, the snapshot inventory, the prune plan's physical-bytes accounting (so the reported reclaim counts hidden files it deletes), the prune entry sweep's residue scan, the archive-expansion temporary folder, the restorer's pool scan and its snapshot-folder listing (so a hidden snapshot folder or hidden pool file stays recoverable). Reparse-point and symlink traversal semantics are unchanged: hidden capture does not follow links. The shell restorer already enumerates dot-files and does not follow links, both by intent (SR-057).

Title: Content-addressed copy with owner election and intra-run memo
Detail: Every stored object is named from its content. Each (hash, length) group elects an owner (the shortest RelativePath, ties broken ordinally), whose extension and storage-form decision (LLR-086) define the group's single physical form; the first member writes it, and every later member in the same run adopts it. The storage-form decision is made lazily and once per group: only on first entry to the write path, never before, and remembered for the rest of the group. Laziness keeps deduplication hits and same-run twins from probing at all, because they never reach the write path; remembering keeps a group whose first member's copy fails from re-probing and re-warning once per failing member. Nothing reads the form before the write path.

Title: Superseded-data preservation after copy/evict, survival tested against the final manifest
Detail: Preserving superseded data runs after the copy and evict steps (nothing is overwritten, because every object is named from its content) and asks whether any row in the FINAL index still claims the old row's DataPath, the same claim test eviction uses (B9). Testing by DataPath is conservative in the direction that matters: a claim always keeps its bytes in the pool. Where one content is stored under two names, the unclaimed one is at worst parked in the newest snapshot, still inside the restore pool. Frozen rows (SR-055/SR-057) and rows whose copy failed keep their claim in the final index, so their objects stay in the pool. There is one code path.

Title: Sanitize kept; legacy store refused by engine AND both restorers
Detail: No backup run migrates the storage layout. Before mutation the run checks the index for unreferenced and missing data (the sanitize step) through the one linear orphan scan (SR-064). A row carrying StoredAsHashSize='Original' fails the set before mutation, with the remedy of starting a fresh backup path. Both restorers scan the authority index before the target exists and refuse with the precondition code (2) when any row carries StoredAsHashSize='Original' (the authoritative marker, matching the engine) or a DataPath containing a path separator (the structural marker, which still catches a store whose column was lost). Nothing is written.

Title: Manifest-derived browse view generator
Detail: Generates a browse view under the resolved view root (by default <BackupPath>_View): a tab-separated index, one HTML page per folder and a root search page. Entry names come from the row: RelativePath, plus '.7z' exactly when the row's Compressed is 'Yes'. The view carries a stamp that is a SHA-256 of the canonical index ROWS, deliberately not the index witness, because a manifest-identical run can rewrite the CSV with different quoting. The generator refuses a view root that is on another volume or that overlaps any owned path in either direction, and, as an independent second guard, refuses to wipe a view root holding anything that is not a generated view. View code lives only in the engine; the shared library never grows it (AGENTS.md section 3).

Title: Linear unreferenced-data audit
Detail: The unreferenced-data audit builds one lookup of referenced DataPaths and checks each on-disk file against it, rather than re-scanning the index per file, so the audit is linear. The lookup compares paths the way the filesystem does, so a case-differing pair on Linux is not conflated.

Title: Config contract v2: removed-key refusal and view keys
Detail: The configuration schema version is 2. PreserveFolderTree is not in the closed key set, and a configuration that carries it is refused with a named diagnostic (not the generic unknown-key message) for JSON and CLIXML alike. BrowseView and ViewPath are in the key set with their vocabulary and placement checks. CompressProbe is in the key set with the same treatment as every optional key (LLR-042): exact-lowercase vocabulary off, excluded-extensions, always, defaulting to always. An optional key with a default is additive, so ConfigVersion stays 2; an older build refusing such a key by name is the closed schema working as designed, not a break.

Title: -Action View dispatch
Detail: -Action View forces a rebuild of the browse view and reports through the SR-040 status table; the backup run also refreshes the view at its end.

Title: Directory sidecar: empty directories and folder attributes
Detail: The source walk, including hidden entries, records each directory that is EMPTY of files or carries a recorded attribute, with its RelativePath and attributes. Emptiness is decided from the ancestors of the file rows the walk already produced, never by re-enumerating each directory, so the pass stays linear in directories plus file rows (the SR-064 discipline). A directory the walk could not enumerate is NOT recorded, because claiming empty for an unreadable directory would be a lie in the dangerous direction; a non-portable directory name (SR-055) is skipped with a warning rather than failing the set a second time. The recorded attributes are Hidden, System, ReadOnly and NotContentIndexed, the only four that can be applied to a directory: Archive, Temporary and Offline are meaningless on one, and Compressed, Encrypted, ReparsePoint and the ReFS integrity bits cannot be set that way at all. Rows sort ordinally, so two runs over the same state write byte-identical sidecars. The directory sidecar (DIRECTORIES.csv) is written beside the index after the index, and is removed when there are no rows, so a tree with no empty or attributed directory is byte-identical to a store without the feature. The prior sidecar is copied into staging so a snapshot keeps its own point in time; it is deliberately not in the kit-artifact list. Both restorers apply it LAST, after every file is written and verified: directories are created parents first and attributes applied deepest first, path traversal is refused as it is for index rows, and the shell restorer creates the directories but reports the Windows attributes as inapplicable on POSIX rather than dropping them silently. The sidecar is advisory and unwitnessed: absent, unreadable or malformed, it leaves exactly the behaviour of a store without it and never fails a restore.

Title: Restored files carry their own modification time
Detail: Both restorers apply the row's own LastWriteTimeStr after the SR-056 (hash, length) verification passes, including after a hash-recovery retry, so a file that was deleted and rewritten never keeps a stamp from the failed attempt. The time is parsed from the index's ISO-8601 round-trip form; where a userland cannot take fractional seconds, the shell restorer retries with them stripped. Stamping is never fatal: the bytes are correct and verified by the time it runs, so a blank or unparseable cell warns and the row still counts as restored. A read-only file does not block it, because setting a file's time needs only the right to write its attributes, which a read-only file grants. This stops a deduplicated row from inheriting the pool object's timestamp; when the time rode along with the copy, every twin got the owner's.

Title: Bounded copy retry with a per-run budget
Detail: Copying a content group's object is retried in attempt rounds: each round tries every member of the group, then waits and retries the whole list. The waits are 250 ms and then 1000 ms, so three attempts cost at most 1.25 s of waiting per file. Only the refusal to write onto a directory at the destination is treated as permanent, since waiting cannot change it; every other failure is treated as possibly transient, because guessing wrong that way costs time while guessing wrong the other way costs the file. The destination is cleared between rounds, so a retry never lands on or merges into partial debris (SR-004). The retry budget belongs to the set: one budget per set is shared by every group, so a systemically unreadable tree cannot sleep the run away; a direct call without a budget gets a fresh local one. On exhaustion the error names the attempt count and states that the file is NOT in the backup; no row is added for it, and the run is marked unsuccessful. A row from an EARLIER run survives untouched, the same frozen-row treatment SR-055/SR-057 give a file the walk could not read.

Title: Byte-derived stored form in the kit
Detail: The stored-form test used by the restorers lives in the shared library, because the restore kit does not bundle the engine (where the audit-side equivalent lives). Cheapest test first: no 7-Zip signature in the first six bytes returns Raw conclusively, since the engine never writes a compressed object without one; a signature with a length different from the row's Length returns Archive on a stat alone; equal lengths hash the file, and a match against the row's xxH2Hash returns Raw because the bytes ARE the content (the user's own archive). An unreadable object returns Raw rather than guessing, so the caller's copy attempt surfaces the real I/O error. Both restorers decide a DataPath-resolved row's form with this test instead of the row's Compressed column; a hash-recovered row keeps the form the pool lookup proved (SR-050). The shell restorer's twin reads the signature with standard coreutils and reuses its XXH128 wrapper. The Compressed column survives in the 9-column schema and still feeds the capacity ESTIMATE in both restorers, which is explicitly approximate and warns when compressed rows exist.

Title: Base-57 name codec and the one canonical parser
Detail: The object-name codec encodes hex to base-57 and refuses an encoding wider than its field rather than keeping the rightmost characters, because a truncated name cannot be checked against the index it addresses. Decoding normalises to an exact hex width, removing any spurious sign digit and restoring leading zeros, and refuses a field wider than the target. A name is built as "<hash22>_<len><ext>". There is exactly one parser: the first 22 characters are the hash, the separator sits at index 22, base-57 digits run to the first dot, and the remainder is an opaque extension that must be free of path separators; a malformed name yields 'no parse', never an error. Two predicates answer different questions: 'is this the current grammar?' and 'is this a RETIRED grammar?' (the structural half of the SR-061 legacy gate). The retired-grammar test is a positive test, never the negation of the first, so a damaged DataPath stays repairable rather than being taken for a legacy store. The shell restorer carries only the retired-grammar predicate (structural; it uses no decoded value) and no current-grammar predicate, which would be dead weight in a file bundled into every backup, since the pool locator matches content rather than names. The PowerShell and shell retired-grammar predicates agree on every name.

Title: The stored extension is opaque and may be empty
Detail: The stored name's extension may be empty: a source file with no extension (README, LICENSE, Makefile) is backed up normally and never fails the set, with compression on or off. The owner's extension is carried verbatim, never validated against the SR-069 alphabet, and the name parser preserves it byte for byte.

Title: POSIX size, temp, time and space shims
Detail: The shell restorer measures a file's size portably across GNU, BSD and POSIX userlands. It selects a measuring style once, by probing a known regular file, and accepts a style only when its output is numeric, because a style that ignores its argument would otherwise succeed on a working directory holding a file named like its format string; it falls back to the POSIX byte count. Temporary directories are always created from an explicit template (GNU supplies a default, BSD does not), and every caller checks the result, because an unchecked failure leaves the path empty and once wrote the 7-Zip self-test probe to the filesystem root. Current-time stamps use an explicit POSIX format. Where the native time-setting form is unavailable, a restored file's modification time is still set exactly for EVERY ISO-8601 offset, by carrying the offset as a POSIX TZ value (whose sign is the inverse of ISO-8601, so '-06:00' becomes 'UTC+6:00'), rather than refusing any offset other than UTC or the host's, which would silently drop SR-066 on BSD for any store written in another timezone.

Title: Canonicalisation that refuses rather than guesses
Detail: Path canonicalisation in the shell restorer resolves a path physically where the platform can; otherwise it REFUSES any path containing a '..' component and reports failure rather than returning its raw input. Lexical '..' reduction is not path resolution: with a symlink outside -> backup, link/../backup/x resolves INSIDE the backup by kernel semantics but OUTSIDE lexically, so reducing first would walk a restore into the root SR-009 protects. The containment test is TRI-STATE (inside, outside, indeterminate) because the safe branch differs by caller: the target guard refuses unless the target is provably OUTSIDE the backup, and the traversal guards reject a path unless it is provably INSIDE the target. Every canonicalisation call site handles failure, including the sidecar containment case, where an empty result would leave the glob '/*' and match every absolute path.

Title: Target-prompt decision core and its dialogs
Detail: The decision whether to prompt for a restore target, and how, is PURE: every signal is an input and the answer is None, Text or Gui, so the whole matrix can be exercised without a dialog. The interactive folder picker is the I/O shell around it: its picker is injectable for tests, it never throws, and when the current thread is not in a single-threaded apartment (PowerShell 7.0 to 7.2 default to multi-threaded) it shows the dialog from a runspace created in a single-threaded apartment. It must not use a bare thread without a runspace: a PowerShell script block on such a thread raises an unhandled exception that terminates the process. Platform dialogs: the Windows folder browser, macOS 'choose folder', zenity, kdialog. The shell restorer's picker is reached ONLY via --pick-target and honours FILEBACKUP_PICKER, invoked quoted so a picker path containing spaces is not split, so tests can drive it headlessly. A cancelled or missing dialog leaves the target empty, and the existing required-argument check then prints usage and exits 2.

Title: Launcher generation and the window hold
Detail: The kit's Windows launcher, RECONSTRUCT.cmd, is CRLF, ASCII, and a single pwsh line passing -ExitCode and all its arguments; reconstruct.command is copied beside it. The .cmd is a PURE PASSTHROUGH and never pauses, because a pause also fires for a console-attached automated caller that passes no arguments and hangs it without returning its exit code. Holding a double-clicked window open is the restorer's job instead, and only when the target came from a picker or a prompt, so the hold can never reach automation. reconstruct.command changes to its own folder (Finder starts it in the home folder), adds --pick-target when given no arguments, and invokes the restorer through 'bash --', so the shell restorer needs no executable bit.

Title: Seven-artifact kit, with the legacy name still recognised
Detail: One kit artifact list of seven names serves the kit deposit, snapshot staging and the kit refresh (-RefreshKits). The retired launcher name RECONSTRUCT.bat is never written but stays in the root-level infrastructure set permanently: a snapshot keeps the kit it was written with, so every older store still holds a RECONSTRUCT.bat, and dropping the name would make every run report it as an orphan or not-in-index row (SR-022). The kit refresh copies and never deletes, so a refreshed older store legitimately holds both launcher names.

Title: One kit revision, pinned so it cannot drift again
Detail: Both restorers carry a '# KitRevision: <n>' marker with the same value. The marker moves whenever a kit-bundled file changes behaviour (AGENTS.md section 3), including the shared library when the change does not touch restore logic. One reader reads it from a folder's bundled PowerShell restorer. The marker records what a BUNDLED kit does, and a deployed copy cannot be rewritten, so a marker found to be wrong is corrected forward to the next number, never back-dated. The two markers are kept equal.

Title: Restores never inherit a read-only pool
Detail: Both restorers clear the read-only attribute on every file they write, at the single write point so the expand path is covered too, and BEFORE the SR-056 verification and the SR-066 timestamp so both act on a writable file. Copying propagates the read-only attribute or mode bits from the source, so a write-protected store would otherwise hand its protection to the restored tree. For the same reason a source file that was read-only at backup time is not restored read-only: read-only state is not part of what a restore reproduces.

Title: Root-level volume pseudo-folder exclusion
Detail: A path is a volume-root pseudo-folder when its FIRST relative segment is one of the volume-root skip names (System Volume Information, $RECYCLE.BIN) AND the root it is relative to is itself a filesystem volume root; the folder and its contents are one test. Without the volume-root condition, a user's own folder of the same name would be excluded and its files silently lost. The test lives in the shared library so the engine and the standalone restorer use one definition. The engine's data enumeration filters BOTH the returned files and the enumeration-error records: the first stops recycle-bin contents being backed up, the second stops 'System Volume Information' marking the set failed. The restorer's pool scan filters both its candidate list and its enumeration errors; filtering only one would leave half the false verdict in place. The shell restorer's twin is a no-op on a native POSIX filesystem but correct on a mounted NTFS volume; it decides volume-root status from the system's mount points and answers 'not a volume root' when detection fails, the safe direction: scan rather than skip.

Title: Physical path containment for the target guard
Detail: The restore-target containment test resolves BOTH paths physically before comparing: it walks up to the deepest EXISTING ancestor, resolves that ancestor's link target when it is a reparse point, and re-appends the non-existent tail, which is sound because a path that does not exist cannot contain a link. Lexical normalisation alone normalises separators and '..' but never follows a junction, so 'C:\outside\link\restore', where 'link' is a junction to the backup, would compare as OUTSIDE and the restore would write into the backup. This matches the shell restorer's canonicalisation (LLR-072).

Title: Staging owner record, heartbeat and lock classifier
Detail: The staging-lock ownership helpers belong to the backup-only engine, not the shared library: the library is bundled into every restore kit, so a change there would move both kit-revision markers, and staging-lock ownership has no restore-side meaning. The rule is a dependency direction (the library must not depend on the engine), not a demand that engine concepts move down. Owner record: a once-only JSON payload (SchemaVersion, Kind, a fresh-GUID RunId, set name, host, container id, boot id, pid, StartedUtc, HeartbeatIntervalSeconds, StaleAfterSeconds 1800) written DIRECTLY to RUN.inprogress by a create-new open: one kernel operation that both creates the file and proves exclusivity, with no temporary file and no rename. A temporary write plus a non-overwriting rename is check-then-rename on Unix and so not exclusive there, its atomic variant needs hard links that exFAT lacks, and a crash mid-publish would strand a temporary file in a folder the run may no longer own, which every later classification would read as HoldsContent, a permanent wedge. The record is written only after the staging area was created successfully; a create-new collision is lock-lost, and the caller aborts touching nothing. Torn reads stay safe on the reader side: ParseInvalid with a fresh modification time classifies OwnerLive and refuses. Every marker read goes through one share-tolerant reader, so the heartbeat's open handle cannot make the engine's own fence and classifier reads fail. A read returns its state (Parsed, ParseInvalid or Unreadable), the record, its last-write time and its age; ParseInvalid with the time fields populated is a normal, expected answer (a torn record is exactly a dead writer), while Unreadable is distinct and refuses upstream. The classifier is PURE of I/O decisions: it takes the caller's forced, fail-closed listing and the record and returns one of Empty, EmptyFresh, OwnerStale, OwnerLive, PruneHeld, HoldsContent or Indeterminate, so the whole matrix can be exercised with no filesystem. The roughly 90 s confirmation sample belongs to the caller (LLR-017), which is what keeps the classifier pure. Heartbeat: the beat runs on its own timer, independent of the run's pipeline, so a long hash cannot starve it and a beat can never terminate the process. Starting it performs ONE synchronous beat before the timer is armed and refuses when that touch did not land: a store that rejects setting a modification time would otherwise beat into an unseen error, and after StaleAfterSeconds a live run would read as dead and be confirmed dead, because the confirmation sample detects change and nothing changes. The running heartbeat is kept reachable for the lock's whole lifetime, because an unreachable timer can be collected and stop silently, and nothing else would report it. Each beat re-reads the marker and touches it only when the RunId is its own, holding one open handle across the check and the touch and setting the time through that handle, so the touch lands on the very file the identity check verified; checking and then touching by path would let a reclaim landing between the two freshen the successor's marker. Stopping it reports the error count and last error when either is nonzero (a beat that fails mid-run cannot be made fatal but must not be invisible); it is idempotent, does not throw on a cleanup path, and DRAINS: it cancels, disposes the timer and waits out any in-flight beat, so no touch can land after Stop returns. The reclaim protocol these helpers serve has an exact order: (1) classify, with the confirmation sample on the stale branches; (2) move the staging area aside to Temp.stale-<utc>-<8 hex>, refusing on failure with no retry loop; (3) create a fresh staging area and IMMEDIATELY publish the new record, refusing on either failure and leaving the aside folder; (4) re-list the aside folder forced and fail-closed, delete the exact marker by name and then the folder non-recursively, keeping the folder on anything else, any I/O error, or either delete failing. Step 4 is the safety proof, not belt and braces: a frozen-then-resumed owner can write between steps 1 and 2, and a non-recursive delete is structurally incapable of taking a data file with it. The fence points are the FIVE phase boundaries of a backup run (before the staging index write, before eviction, before preserving superseded data, before the backup root's index publish and before the snapshot publish), where a marker whose RunId differs means the lock was lost and the run aborts cleaning up nothing; an unreadable marker is first retried three times about 300 ms apart. The staging OS lock (LLR-090) is a separate primitive and changes nothing here: the classifier is never told whether that lock is held, so holding it can never turn a verdict into a reclaimable one.

Title: Sampled compressibility probe and composed storage-form decision
Detail: The probe and the storage-form decision belong to the backup-only engine, never the shared library: the library is bundled into every restore kit, so placing them there would move both kit-revision markers for a concept restore has no use for, and the architectural rule is a dependency direction (the library must not depend on the engine), not a demand that engine concepts move down. Probe. The probe opens the source read-only, sharing reads only, the same sharing the hashing and stored-form reads use, so a successful probe predicts a successful copy. It returns 'no measurement' for any path it cannot open; that is a normal, expected answer, not an error. What that sharing buys is platform-qualified. On Windows a read-shared open fails while any writer holds the file, so the probe cannot sample a file open for writing. On POSIX file sharing is advisory, so a non-cooperating writer can change bytes under the sample; against that, and against a Windows writer that opens after the probe does, the probe reads the file's length and last-write time before and after sampling and returns 'no measurement' if either moved. The worst case is the list's answer. Geometry: with 256 KiB windows and three samples, a file shorter than three windows is read once, whole, as a single sample, which avoids over-reading files between 256 KiB and 768 KiB; otherwise three windows are taken at offsets 0, (len - 256 KiB) / 2 (rounded down) and len - 256 KiB, each filled completely unless end of file is reached first. Each window is compressed into a counting sink and its compressed size is read only after the encoder is closed, because a count taken earlier reads short and would call random bytes compressible. The probe reports the sampled and compressed byte totals plus the per-window ratios for the log line. An empty file is below the floor and never probed. Decision. The storage-form decision is a pure function with no I/O. Its inputs are: compression enabled, the set's CompressProbe mode (off, excluded-extensions or always), the already-compressed list's opinion (taken as if compression were enabled, so it carries only the list's view), the length, the size floor, the sampled and compressed byte counts, and the threshold. It returns whether to compress and a Reason in {CompressDisabled, ModeOff, BelowFloor, ListExempt, ProbeUnavailable, ProbeCompressible, ProbeIncompressible}, evaluating SR-081's ordered rule. There is no name-based override, so no input and no Reason is named after a format. Compression disabled is tested FIRST, and with it nothing is read at all. The ruled defaults are held in the engine: a file must shrink by at least 10 percent in aggregate (compressed / original <= 0.90) to be compressed, and files below 256 KiB are never probed. Neither is configurable (SR-081: two knobs nobody can measure), and the shared library exposes neither. Use. The set's CompressProbe value reaches the group copy; a direct call without it uses the default. The decision is made lazily and once per group (LLR-058). Deduplication hits and same-run twins never reach the write path and never probe, which is how SR-061 stays true: no already-stored object's form is ever re-decided. When it does decide, the probe walks the group's candidates, the owner first and then every member (the same list the copy uses, because a locked owner must not fail a group that a readable twin can serve), and samples the first that opens. Only when none opens is the decision ProbeUnavailable, which takes the list's answer with one WARN and never fails the run. Emission: one DEBUG line per written group, 'compress-decision: <rel> <Reason> ratio=<aggregate> windows=<r1,r2,r3>', and three per-set physical-object counters, incremented only after a successful write: 'Probe stored raw: <n> objects, <bytes>', 'Probe compressed: <n>', 'Probe reads: <bytes>'. Codec: Brotli at its fastest level, chosen because it made the fewest wrong decisions against the real whole-file 7-Zip -mx=9 outcome on a calibration corpus, and is also cheaper per sample than Deflate. Deflate's 32 KiB history cannot see a 64 KiB repetition even inside one 256 KiB sample, so it would store raw a file 7-Zip shrinks to nothing. A repetition period longer than a sample window cannot be seen by any codec; that is a limit of sample size and count, and its cost is one file stored raw that could have shrunk, a correct storage form either way (I-1), never a data risk. The decision rule is codec-agnostic.

Title: Atomic Write-Manifest
Detail: The index writer builds the canonical rows and then: (1) deletes any temporary index left beside the destination by an earlier kill (a no-op when absent) and writes the new content to that temporary index, removing the partial file and re-raising on an ordinary failure; (2) publishes it over the destination with a single atomic overwriting rename (rename(2) on Linux, a replace-existing move on Windows), removing the temporary file and re-raising on failure; then (3) writes the witness over the PUBLISHED file, still AFTER the index, so a kill between (2) and (3) leaves a complete index beside a stale witness, which is a loud mismatch (SR-038). Test seams before the temporary write, after it and after the rename stand in for a kill that runs no cleanup. Not done, deliberately: an fsync of the temporary file before the rename, so a power loss (as opposed to a process kill) can still lose the newest write on a filesystem that reorders the rename ahead of the data; the earlier in-place write had no fsync either.

Title: Manifest staging file allowlist and Temp tolerance
Detail: The temporary index name MANIFEST.csv.tmp is root-level infrastructure, beside MANIFEST.csv.meta.tmp, in the backup root and in every snapshot, so the store's data enumeration, which the orphan scan, the storage-form audit and the prune sweep all use, never returns it. (The shell restorer already skips any root-level MANIFEST* name during hash recovery.) The staging-lock classifier ignores exactly that case-sensitive name before testing for unrecognised entries: a staging area holding RUN.inprogress plus the temporary index classifies by the marker alone (OwnerStale or OwnerLive), and one holding only the temporary index is Empty by the directory's modification time; any other entry still yields HoldsContent. Reclaim tolerates it in the aside folder and deletes it by exact name before the marker, and a run's own cleanup counts it among its disposable leaves. It is never the only copy of anything: it is an incomplete copy of a file that still exists beside it.

Title: Staging OS lock primitive
Detail: The staging OS lock is the file Temp.lock in the change root. Taking it opens the file, creating it if absent, with read access and no sharing: refusing all sharing IS the lock, and read-only access means a read-only attribute cannot wedge it. Any failure to open is retried up to 3 times, 250 ms apart, and then refused with a message beginning [SR-075/lock-held]. The platform error only chooses the wording (held by another process, or could not be opened); every branch refuses identically. The message does not use the lost-marker-lock prefix, so it is never mistaken for a lost marker lock. Releasing closes the file, makes a second release a no-op, accepts a lock that was never taken, never throws and never deletes the file. A test seam inside the same open guard stands in for an open failure. The lock belongs to the backup-only engine, which is not part of the restore kit.

Title: Backup holds the OS lock across the no-marker window
Detail: A backup run's opening order is: resolve the set's paths, creating missing roots; take the staging OS lock; read the prior state; create the run log; then set up staging. No read of store state precedes the lock. If the lock cannot be taken, the run appends one refusal line to the set's backup log (appending, never truncating, because the log belongs to the live holder), marks the set failed and returns. The prior-state reads (the last backup time, the guard against a populated index with no last backup time, and the witness gate) keep their order and run under a guard that releases the lock and re-raises the ORIGINAL error, so the witness refusal still maps to exit 3 and the backup log is left as the last run wrote it. Creating the run log is guarded the same way. Staging setup receives the held lock and passes it to reclaim, which only logs that a current-version holder is excluded and that an older FileBackup takes no OS lock; classification, the confirmation sample and the refusals are untouched (SR-086). If staging setup fails, the lock is released first. Otherwise the lock is released in the run's final cleanup, after the heartbeat is stopped and in a way that cannot be skipped; on the healthy path that is after the snapshot is published, run state is written, deduplication and the browse view run, and it also runs on every error and every lock-lost return. Test seams sit right after the marker is deleted and on either side of the snapshot-publishing rename.

Title: Prune holds the same OS lock
Detail: Prune takes the staging OS lock once, after resolving the roots and before working through the named snapshots, and so before committed-residue removal, the rails, the staging-area creation and every re-home, unless -WhatIf is in effect. If the lock cannot be taken, prune reports every named snapshot as Status Refused, Code 2, with a single refusal of kind staging-busy whose message is the [SR-075/lock-held] text, and returns. The lock is held for the whole batch and released in prune's final cleanup. The existing staging-area rail, the create-without-overwrite staging take and PRUNE.inprogress are unchanged. A test seam runs right after PRUNE.inprogress is written.

Title: Lock file lifecycle and invisibility
Detail: Nothing deletes, writes or truncates Temp.lock. Every enumeration of the change root lists directories only (the engine's snapshot inventory additionally filters by the snapshot pattern, and every prune, audit, kit-refresh and -Action Snapshots path reaches the change root through it; both restorers build their pool from directories), so the lock file is invisible to all of them. Committed prune residue and the staging area are addressed by exact name.

Title: Repair and kit refresh hold the same OS lock
Detail: Storage-form repair and the kit refresh hold the same staging OS lock. Taking it for them refuses a blank change root, creates a missing one, and then takes the OS lock; on any failure it logs one ERROR line through the caller's logger and refuses with a message carrying [SR-075/lock-held]. Repair takes it as its FIRST act, before the storage-form audit, so findings and repair see one state; the kit refresh takes it before listing the snapshots. Both skip it under -WhatIf, and both release it in a final cleanup around their whole body. The lock lives in the mutating operations, not in the verify entry point, so a direct module caller is covered; the verify entry point turns the refusal into exit code 2. A read-only -Action Verify runs only the storage-form audit and the pool-resolution check and takes no lock. Left lock-free because they do not write the store: -Action Snapshots, -Action View (it writes only the view root, which the SR-063 rails keep outside both roots), the -Deep audit (its scratch files are under the system temporary directory) and both restorers (they write only the restore target). Every other engine step that writes the store is a backup or prune step reached only from a backup run or a prune; several of those steps can also be called directly as module exports, and such a direct caller holds no lock.
